title: 1 Chronicles 24:1–19
context: The priests, descended from Aaron, are divided into twenty-four courses. Since Nadab and Abihu died without children (compare Leviticus 10:1–2; Numbers 3:4), the priesthood continues through Eleazar and Ithamar, with sixteen family heads from Eleazar and eight from Ithamar. David, with Zadok and Ahimelech, assigns the courses impartially by lot, recorded by the scribe Shemaiah, and the twenty-four names are listed in the order the lots fell. Ahimelech is called the son of Abiathar here, as in 2 Samuel 8:17, while 1 Chronicles 18:16 reads Abimelech and 1 Samuel 22:20 names Abiathar as a son of Ahimelech; the text does not explain the relationship or the spelling. The text does not describe how the lots were cast. The course of Abijah, the eighth, reappears in Luke 1:5, where Zacharias serves in that division. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about fairness, order, and the LORD’s command behind Israel’s worship.

verses.text: These were the divisions of the sons of Aaron. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Aaron listed: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The priestly line is introduced with its full family (compare Exodus 6:23).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as recalling both the privilege and the solemnity of the priesthood. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as the starting point for the priestly courses.

verses.text: But Nadab and Abihu died before their father, and had no children; therefore Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Nadab and Abihu died before their father without children, so Eleazar and Ithamar served. Past judgment shapes the present order.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a sober reminder of the holiness of God’s service (compare Leviticus 10:1–2; Numbers 3:4). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a call to reverent worship.

verses.text: David, with Zadok of the sons of Eleazar and Ahimelech of the sons of Ithamar, divided them according to their ordering in their service.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David, with Zadok of Eleazar’s line and Ahimelech of Ithamar’s line, dividing the priests. Both priestly families share in the organization.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cooperation of king and priests as reflecting ordered leadership under God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as careful planning for worship.

verses.text: There were more chief men found of the sons of Eleazar than of the sons of Ithamar; and they were divided like this: of the sons of Eleazar there were sixteen, heads of fathers’ houses; and of the sons of Ithamar, according to their fathers’ houses, eight.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Eleazar’s line had sixteen heads of households and Ithamar’s eight. The division reflects the actual size of the families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the proportional division as fair and practical. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that order follows real circumstances.

verses.text: Thus they were divided impartially by drawing lots; for there were princes of the sanctuary and princes of God, both of the sons of Eleazar, and of the sons of Ithamar.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests divided impartially by drawing lots, since both lines had leaders of the sanctuary. Fairness guards against favoritism.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lot as a means of leaving decisions to God (compare Proverbs 16:33). Readers in both traditions commonly note that the text does not describe how the lots were cast.

verses.text: Shemaiah the son of Nethanel the scribe, who was of the Levites, wrote them in the presence of the king, the princes, Zadok the priest, Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, and the heads of the fathers’ households of the priests and of the Levites; one fathers’ house being taken for Eleazar, and one taken for Ithamar.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Shemaiah the scribe recording the divisions before the king, priests, and leaders. Public witness ensures accountability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formal recording as part of ordered worship. Both traditions commonly note that Ahimelech is called the son of Abiathar here, as in 2 Samuel 8:17, while 1 Chronicles 18:16 reads Abimelech and 1 Samuel 22:20 names Abiathar as a son of Ahimelech; the text does not explain the relationship or the spelling.

verses.text: Now the first lot came out to Jehoiarib, the second to Jedaiah,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the first lot falling to Jehoiarib and the second to Jedaiah. Each family receives its place in turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the order of the lots as accepted by all. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as the beginning of a careful list.

verses.text: the third to Harim, the fourth to Seorim,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the third and fourth courses assigned to Harim and Seorim. Every family has a set time to serve in turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as reflecting a stable order for worship. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a fair system.

verses.text: the fifth to Malchijah, the sixth to Mijamin,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Malchijah and Mijamin receiving the fifth and sixth courses. Service is shared across many families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shared service as guarding against one family dominating worship. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the ordered rotation.

verses.text: the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hakkoz and Abijah receiving the seventh and eighth courses. The course of Abijah later appears in Luke 1:5.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the continuity of the courses into the New Testament as a link between Israel’s worship and the gospel story (compare Luke 1:8–9). Both traditions commonly value this connection.

verses.text: the ninth to Jeshua, the tenth to Shecaniah,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Jeshua and Shecaniah receiving the ninth and tenth courses. Each name represents a household called to serve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as honoring every family’s place in God’s house. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the complete rotation.

verses.text: the eleventh to Eliashib, the twelfth to Jakim,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Eliashib and Jakim receiving the eleventh and twelfth courses. The first half of the rotation is complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the orderly progression as reflecting God’s care for structure in worship. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a fair arrangement.

verses.text: the thirteenth to Huppah, the fourteenth to Jeshebeab,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Huppah and Jeshebeab receiving the thirteenth and fourteenth courses. The list continues with equal care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see each family receiving its place without distinction of rank. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the impartial system.

verses.text: the fifteenth to Bilgah, the sixteenth to Immer,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Bilgah and Immer receiving the fifteenth and sixteenth courses. Every family is named and remembered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the naming as reflecting God’s knowledge of his servants. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the ordered rotation.

verses.text: the seventeenth to Hezir, the eighteenth to Happizzez,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezir and Happizzez receiving the seventeenth and eighteenth courses. The order is complete and fair.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as reflecting the shared responsibility of the priests. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a careful record.

verses.text: the nineteenth to Pethahiah, the twentieth to Jehezkel,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Pethahiah and Jehezkel receiving the nineteenth and twentieth courses. Service is spread across many households.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the arrangement as ensuring continuous worship. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the organized priesthood.

verses.text: the twenty-first to Jachin, the twenty-second to Gamul,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Jachin and Gamul receiving the twenty-first and twenty-second courses. The rotation nears completion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the steady progression as reflecting God’s orderly provision. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the full list.

verses.text: the twenty-third to Delaiah, and the twenty-fourth to Maaziah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Delaiah and Maaziah receiving the twenty-third and twenty-fourth courses. The twenty-four courses are complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the completed list as a framework for continuous worship. Both traditions commonly read the verse as concluding the priestly divisions.

verses.text: This was their ordering in their service, to come into the LORD’s house according to the ordinance given to them by Aaron their father, as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the courses ordered according to the ordinance given by Aaron, as the LORD commanded. The structure rests on God’s word, not human preference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the arrangement as grounded in God’s command (compare 1 Chronicles 6:49). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a reminder that worship is shaped by God’s instruction (compare 1 Corinthians 14:40).
